maml:description.maml:para: Adds a client application to the applications kept for the session.

Posh-MSAL keeps a list of client applications for the session so that Get-MsalToken and Select-MsalClientApplication reuse them, and with them their token caches. This cmdlet adds an application built with New-MsalClientApplication to that list.
Adding an application already in the list is an error (AddMsalClientApplicationFailureAlreadyExists).

maml:description.maml:para: Forgets the client applications kept for the session, or deletes the token cache on disk.
Without FromDisk, empties the session's list of client applications: their tokens held in memory are lost, and the next Get-MsalToken builds new applications.

With FromDisk, deletes the token caches on disk instead and leaves the session's list alone: the user and app caches, encrypted and unencrypted, their keyring entries on Linux, and the old MSAL.PS cache file, so that it is not copied again. Applications enabled with Enable-MsalTokenCacheOnDisk then read an empty cache.

maml:description.maml:para: Makes a client application keep its tokens on disk, encrypted, across sessions.

Registers the application's token caches with the Posh-MSAL cache on disk, shared by every application and every PowerShell session of the user, through Microsoft.Identity.Client.Extensions.Msal. The cache is encrypted with DPAPI on Windows and kept in the keyring (libsecret) on Linux, in the Posh-MSAL folder of LocalApplicationData. Signed-in accounts go to the user token cache; the tokens of confidential clients go to a separate app token cache.
The first time on Windows, an MSAL.PS cache found in the MSAL.PS folder of LocalApplicationData is copied into the user token cache; the old file is not changed.

When the cache cannot be encrypted, as on Linux without a keyring (SSH or headless sessions), the cmdlet fails with MsalTokenCacheNotProtected unless AllowUnencryptedStorage is given; it then keeps a plain file readable by the user's account, and says so with a warning.
On a platform with no cache on disk, it warns and the tokens stay in memory.

maml:description.maml:para: Gets an OAuth token from Microsoft Entra ID, in the public cloud or a sovereign cloud.

Gets a token through MSAL.NET for a public client (a user signs in) or a confidential client (the application signs in with a secret, a certificate or an assertion). Unless an application is piped in, the cmdlet uses the session's application for these settings, as Select-MsalClientApplication does, so the tokens it caches are reused by later calls.

The flow follows the parameters. A confidential client uses the client credentials, or the authorization code with AuthorizationCode, or on-behalf-of with UserAssertion. A public client signs in with UserCredential (username and password), DeviceCode, Interactive, IntegratedWindowsAuth or Silent; with none of them, it tries the token cache, then integrated Windows authentication, then an interactive sign-in. Integrated Windows authentication and username and password are deprecated by MSAL.NET and warn when asked for.

The cloud comes from Environment, AzureCloudInstance or Authority (the public cloud by default); parameters that point at different clouds are an error. Without Scopes, the scope is the Graph endpoint of the cloud followed by /.default. On an application piped in, only the tenant can change per request.

Interactive sign-in uses MSAL's embedded window on Windows PowerShell 5.1 and the system browser on PowerShell 7, which needs an http://localhost redirect URI on the app registration; without one, PowerShell 7 falls back to device code. With the system browser, the cmdlet gives up after 2 minutes unless Timeout says otherwise. Device code messages go to the information stream.
A failure is a terminating error: GetMsalTokenFailureAuthenticationError (the MSAL.NET exception is in the error record), GetMsalTokenFailureOperationTimeout or GetMsalTokenFailureOperationStopped.

maml:description.maml:para: Builds a public or confidential client application for one cloud and tenant.

Returns a new MSAL.NET client application, to pass to Get-MsalToken or to keep for the session with Add-MsalClientApplication. Without a credential it is a public client, for users signing in; with ClientSecret, ClientCertificate (with ClientClaims or not) or ClientAssertion it is a confidential client. MSAL.NET application options can be piped in instead of ClientId.

The authority comes from Environment, AzureCloudInstance or Authority, with TenantId (the public cloud and the common tenant by default); parameters that point at different clouds are an error. An application signs in to one cloud only: Get-MsalToken refuses a request for another.

Without RedirectUri, a public client gets MSAL's default redirect URI; on Windows PowerShell 5.1 it is the nativeclient page of the chosen cloud's authority host. AuthenticationBroker makes it sign in through the Windows broker (WAM).
This cmdlet does not keep the application: Get-MsalToken and Select-MsalClientApplication build and keep their own.
